title.title: How Smart Contracts Work
title.subtitle: What happens when a smart contract runs: the Web3 stack, one escrow deal stepped through live, quick gas and token recaps, and oracles, a contract's only window on the real world. Code stays optional.

stackExercise.heading: Build the dApp Stack
stackExercise.promptIdle: Click a component, then click its layer to place it.
stackExercise.promptSelectedA: Now click a layer to place
stackExercise.infoHovered: Hover any placed component to see what it is.
stackExercise.infoIdle: Every component carries a one-line definition. Click one for more detail, then click a layer to place it.

frontend.label: Frontend Layer
frontend.desc: What the user sees and interacts with

metamask.label: Wallet
metamask.gloss: Holds your keys and signs transactions.
metamask.info: A wallet (Rabby, Zerion, MetaMask, …) that stores your keys and signs transactions in the frontend. It never custodies funds on a server.

react.label: React / Next.js
react.gloss: The web interface the user sees and clicks.
react.info: The UI framework that renders the dApp interface in the browser. It holds no on-chain logic — it just calls contracts through a wallet or RPC.

infura.label: Infura RPC
infura.gloss: A hosted gateway between apps and blockchain nodes.
infura.info: A hosted RPC gateway that lets apps read state and broadcast transactions without running their own node. It exposes the blockchain over a normal HTTPS endpoint.

solidity.label: Solidity Contract
solidity.gloss: The contract's code: the dApp's rules.
solidity.info: The smart-contract source code that defines the dApp's on-chain rules and state. Once compiled and deployed, it lives on-chain and runs on every node.

evm.label: EVM
evm.gloss: Runs contract code identically on every node.
evm.info: The Ethereum Virtual Machine executes contract bytecode deterministically. It is the runtime baked into every node, so all of them reach the same result.

pos.label: PoS Validators
pos.gloss: Stakers who order transactions and confirm blocks.
pos.info: Validators stake ETH to propose and attest blocks under Proof of Stake. They are the on-chain consensus layer that orders and finalises transactions.

ipfs.label: IPFS
ipfs.gloss: Decentralised file storage for data too big or costly to keep on-chain.
ipfs.info: IPFS (InterPlanetary File System) is a peer-to-peer network for storing files such as images and documents. Storing them on-chain would cost a fortune, so the contract keeps only the file's fingerprint (its hash) and the file itself lives on IPFS.

thegraph.label: The Graph
thegraph.gloss: Indexes blockchain data so apps can query it quickly.
thegraph.info: The Graph is an indexing service. A blockchain is slow to search, so The Graph reads contract events as they happen and organises them into a database-style API that an app can query in milliseconds.

chainlink.label: Chainlink Oracle
chainlink.gloss: An oracle network: brings real-world data on-chain.
chainlink.info: Chainlink is an oracle network: independent computers that fetch real-world data, such as prices, and write it on-chain. A contract cannot fetch that data itself. Why not, and what can go wrong, is the 🔮 Oracles chapter later in this section.

web3.heading: The Web3 Landscape
web3.subtitle: A shift in where trust is placed.

before.title: Trust intermediaries
before.note: You trust that the intermediary is honest, solvent, and won't be hacked or censored.

after.title: Trust mathematics and transparent code
after.note: You trust the protocol — not the people running it.

implication.title: Implication: Disintermediation
implication.body: When code enforces the rules, middlemen become optional. Smart contracts can replace escrow agents, brokers, settlement systems and notaries.

standards.bridge: a token is simply a smart contract that follows a shared template, so every wallet, exchange and app can plug into it with no custom work.

components.heading: Anatomy of a Smart Contract
components.subtitle: Five building blocks. You do not need to read the code; the five terms are the vocabulary.

cards.title: Code
cards.desc: The business logic and conditional statements. Written in Solidity (Ethereum), Rust (Solana), or Vyper. Once deployed, the code is immutable.

cards.title: State
cards.desc: Stored data that the contract maintains and modifies over time. Examples: token balances, ownership records, vote counts. Persisted on-chain.

cards.title: Functions
cards.desc: Specific operations callable by external parties or other contracts. Can be read-only (free) or state-changing (costs gas).

cards.title: Events
cards.desc: Logs that record important contract activities. Emitted when key actions occur — cheaply stored and readable by off-chain systems.

cards.title: Blockchain Platform
cards.desc: The execution environment. Ethereum, Polygon, Solana, BNB Chain… Each has different performance, cost, and tooling trade-offs.

components.pickHint: Click a building block to find it in the code
components.platformBody: this Solidity contract deploys to Ethereum, Polygon, Arbitrum, Base, and any EVM-compatible chain with zero code changes.

workflow.heading: How Smart Contracts Work
workflow.subtitle: Every run follows the same five steps, from deployment to notification.

steps.label: Deploy
steps.desc: Contract code is compiled and uploaded to the blockchain. It gets a permanent address — immutable from this point on.

steps.label: Trigger
steps.desc: A user or system sends a transaction to the contract address, calling a function with the required inputs.

steps.label: Execute
steps.desc: The EVM (or equivalent VM) runs the contract code on every node in the network simultaneously.

steps.label: Update
steps.desc: State changes are recorded on the blockchain — permanent, transparent, and agreed upon by consensus.

steps.label: Emit
steps.desc: Events are emitted and logged on-chain, notifying off-chain systems (front-ends, indexers, oracles).

workflow.bridge: Five boxes are abstract. Next, follow one real deal, an escrow payment, through every step.

run.heading: What actually happens when a smart contract runs?
run.subtitle: Follow one escrow deal: Ana buys equipment from Rui for 2 ETH, and the money is released only on delivery.

stages.label: Deploy
stages.who: Rui publishes the escrow contract, once.
stages.what: The code goes on-chain and gets a permanent address. It names the buyer, the seller and the 2 ETH price. From here on nobody can edit the rules, Rui included.
stages.biz: Like signing the agreement and handing it to a neutral escrow agent, except the agent is code that cannot be persuaded.

stages.label: Call
stages.who: Ana signs a transaction calling deposit() with 2 ETH.
stages.what: A contract never acts on its own. It sits idle until a signed transaction arrives at its address and names a function to run.
stages.biz: Ana pays into escrow straight from her own wallet. No bank form, no opening hours.

stages.label: Run
stages.who: Every node runs the same code.
stages.what: Before anything moves, the contract checks its rules: is the caller the buyer, and is the amount the agreed price? One failed check cancels the whole transaction.
stages.biz: The compliance check is automatic and identical on thousands of machines.

stages.label: State changes
stages.who: The network records the new state.
stages.what: 2 ETH leaves Ana's wallet and is locked in the contract. The status flips to Funded. This is now the single shared record of the deal.
stages.biz: The money is provably set aside. Neither Ana nor Rui can pull it back alone.

stages.label: Event fires
stages.what: It emits a Deposited event, a public receipt that apps can listen for. Rui's order system sees it and ships the goods.
stages.biz: The notification triggers the next business step, with no phone call and no reconciliation.

stages.label: Done
stages.who: Ana confirms delivery, and the same loop runs again.
stages.what: Her confirmDelivery() call is checked, the 2 ETH moves to Rui, the status becomes Complete and a Released event fires. The deal is settled.
stages.biz: Payment on delivery, settled in minutes, with no escrow agent to pay or to trust.

checks.pass: Both checks pass, so the run continues.
checks.revert: Reverted: nothing changes, and the caller still pays the gas.

run.footnote: Balances leave out gas fees to keep the numbers clean.
run.logEmpty: No events yet. Events are the contract's public receipts.
run.gasNote: Whoever sends the transaction pays for the run.

solidity.pickHint: Hover or click a letter to find it in the code
solidity.heading: Reading a Smart Contract
solidity.subtitle: Optional. You will not write Solidity in this course; one annotated contract shows that it is readable code, not a black box.

annotations.title: Contract Declaration
annotations.desc: Like a class in OOP. All state and functions live inside. Once deployed, this code is immutable at its address on the blockchain.

annotations.title: State Variables
annotations.desc: Stored permanently on-chain. public creates a getter function automatically. Every write costs gas — reads are free.

annotations.title: Mapping (Key→Value Store)
annotations.desc: mapping(address => uint256) is the on-chain equivalent of a database table. Every Ethereum address maps to a token balance. Not iterable — you must know the key.

annotations.title: Event
annotations.desc: Logged to the blockchain but NOT stored in state. Cheap to emit (~375 gas). Indexed fields enable efficient off-chain search. This is how block explorers display token transfers.

annotations.title: Constructor
annotations.desc: Runs exactly once at deployment. Sets the token name, symbol, and total supply. After this, it never runs again — state is locked as deployed.

annotations.title: msg.sender
annotations.desc: The address that called this function — in the constructor, this is the deployer. All initial supply goes to them. A critical security variable: always validate who msg.sender is.

annotations.title: Function
annotations.desc: external means only outside callers can call this (not the contract itself). public allows both external and internal calls. Every function that changes state costs gas.

annotations.title: require (Guard Clause)
annotations.desc: If the condition is false, the entire transaction reverts — no state changes, no gas refund for execution so far. This is the Checks step in Checks-Effects-Interactions.

execution.heading: Execution Environment
execution.subtitle: Why contracts run the same way on every node, and what that rules out.

properties.title: Virtual Machines
properties.subtitle: Isolated execution environments
properties.desc: The EVM (Ethereum), SVM (Solana), WASM (Polkadot, Near)… Each VM is a sandbox that cannot reach the host machine's files, network or memory.

properties.title: Distributed Execution
properties.subtitle: Same code runs on thousands of nodes
properties.desc: When a transaction triggers a smart contract, every full node in the network runs the same code independently. There is no single server — execution is replicated across the globe.
examples: Redundancy eliminates single points of failure
No one can selectively block execution

properties.title: Deterministic Results
properties.subtitle: Identical inputs always produce identical outputs
properties.desc: Smart contracts cannot use randomness, real-time clocks, or external data without special tools. This constraint is what makes distributed consensus possible — every node must agree on the result.

properties.title: Consensus Requirement
properties.subtitle: Majority agreement required for state changes
properties.desc: After execution, nodes compare results. Only if a supermajority agrees on the output does the state change get written to the blockchain. A single malicious node cannot affect the outcome.
examples: PoS: validators attest to execution results

evmCore.title: Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM)
evmCore.desc: The original standard — runs Solidity & Vyper bytecode

execution.deployBody: EVM-compatible chains share the same bytecode standard — one Solidity contract works across 30+ chains.

capabilities.heading: New Capabilities
capabilities.subtitle: Five things that were not possible before.
capabilities.whyBody: no intermediary to pay or trust, global reach by default, public rules anyone can verify, and execution with no office hours.

items.title: Permissionless Composability
items.tagline: Any contract can plug into any other — no API keys, no approval.
items.example: Flash loan: borrow $10M across 3 protocols and repay, in one atomic tx.

items.title: Atomic Transactions
items.tagline: Multi-step operations fully succeed or fully revert — never half-done.
items.example: DEX swap: send ETH → check liquidity → transfer tokens — all or nothing.

items.title: Global Shared State
items.tagline: One synchronized state, readable worldwide, with no central server.
items.example: An NFT's owner is instantly visible to every marketplace and game everywhere.

items.title: Programmable Money
items.tagline: Value with built-in rules — "pay only if delivery is confirmed."
items.example: Superfluid streams salary by the second — no payroll department.

items.title: Censorship Resistance
items.tagline: No government, company, or dev can block a valid transaction.
items.example: OFAC blacklisted Tornado Cash — the front-end died, the contract ran on.

liquidity.heading: Why let crypto sit idle when it could earn interest?
liquidity.subtitle: A lending pool: holders deposit, borrowers draw from the same pot, and the interest flows back to the holders. No bank in the middle.
liquidity.poolSub: a smart contract · amounts in USDC
holderStatus: ✓ In the pool, ready to be lent
poolStatus: 40% lent out, backed by locked ETH
Open to the next depositor or borrower

steps.label: Idle
steps.what: A holder has 10,000 USDC sitting in a wallet. Like cash under a mattress, it earns nothing. A bank could lend it out, but the bank decides who qualifies, and takes its cut.

steps.label: Deposit
steps.what: The holder sends the 10,000 USDC to the pool's smart contract. No application, no opening hours. It joins 90,000 USDC from other depositors, and the contract records a 10% share of the pool.

steps.label: Borrow
steps.what: A borrower wants 40,000 USDC. There is no credit check; instead the borrower locks ETH worth $60,000 as collateral, more than the loan. The contract releases the USDC at once. If the collateral's value falls too far, the contract allows it to be sold to repay the pool.

steps.label: Repay
steps.what: Later the borrower repays the 40,000 plus 2,000 in interest (5%), and the contract releases the collateral. The interest stays in the pool: 100,000 has become 102,000.

steps.label: Yield
steps.what: The holder withdraws a 10% share of the now bigger pool: 10,200 USDC. The extra 200 is the yield, paid entirely by the borrower. Borrowers paid 5% and depositors earned 2%, because only 40% of the pool was out on loan. Nobody approved or processed anything: the contract did.

why.title: Idle assets earn.
why.desc: The yield is the borrowers' interest, shared by everyone in the pool.

why.title: No gatekeeper.
why.desc: Anyone with a wallet can deposit or borrow. No bank, no application.

why.title: Collateral replaces trust.
why.desc: The contract never asks who you are; it only checks what you locked.

liquidity.risk: a bug in the contract, or a wrong price for the collateral, can cost depositors money.
liquidity.footnote: Illustrative numbers. Real pools (Aave, Compound) set the rate by formula: the more of the pool is borrowed, the higher it climbs, and the protocol keeps a small cut.
liquidity.bridge: the one loan from a pool like this that needs no collateral at all.

flash.heading: How do you borrow $10 million with no collateral at all?
flash.subtitle: A flash loan: borrowed, used across three protocols and repaid inside one single transaction. If the repayment fails, none of it ever happened.
flash.txSub: signed once · shown in slow motion · on-chain it all lands in a single block

steps.label: Before the transaction
steps.what: A trader spots the same asset at two prices: ETH costs $2,000 on DEX A and $2,010 on DEX B. Buying low and selling high would pay, but it takes millions to matter, and the trader has nothing. Everything that follows is one transaction, shown in slow motion.

steps.label: Borrow
steps.what: Call 1 goes to a lending pool like the one on the previous slide, only far bigger, and takes out $10M. No collateral, no credit check, no questions. The pool's code allows it on one condition: the money, plus a $5,000 fee, must be back before this transaction ends.

steps.label: Buy low
steps.what: Call 2 goes to a second protocol, DEX A, and swaps the $10M for 5,000 ETH at $2,000. DEX A never agreed to work with the lending pool; nobody asked its permission. That is permissionless composability.

steps.label: Sell high
steps.what: Call 3 goes to a third protocol, DEX B, and sells the 5,000 ETH at $2,010 for $10.05M. Three independent protocols, chained by one caller, in one transaction.
steps.whatFail: Call 3 goes to DEX B, but another trader got there first and the price gap has closed: the 5,000 ETH fetch only $9.98M. The transaction is now short.

steps.label: Repay
steps.what: Call 4 sends $10,005,000 back to the pool. The pool checks its balance: all there, plus the fee. Every call held, so the transaction is confirmed and the trader keeps $45,000, having put in no capital beyond the gas fee.
steps.whatFail: Call 4 needs $10,005,000, but only $9.98M is there. The pool's check fails and, because a transaction is atomic, every earlier call is undone: no sale, no purchase, no loan. The pool never lost a cent; the trader loses only the gas fee.

flash.toggleLabel: Try it: does the repayment arrive?

composability.title: Permissionless Composability
composability.desc: Protocols snap together like money legos: one contract calls another, which calls another, and nobody's permission is needed.

atomicity.title: Atomic Transactions
atomicity.desc: All or nothing: either every step succeeds, or the entire transaction reverts as if it never happened.

flash.bridge: anyone can command millions for one transaction, attackers included. This is how price-feed oracle attacks are funded, as the Oracles chapter shows next.
flash.footnote: Illustrative numbers; price impact and gas ignored. The 0.05% fee is Aave V3's default.

gas.heading: Gas: the 10-second version
gas.lead: You saw gas and EIP-1559 in Platforms §2. Here is all you need for this course: every step of the run you just watched had a price.

formula.workSub: gas units: more computation and storage, more gas
formula.priceSub: set by demand: it rises when the network is busy
formula.feeSub: paid in ETH by whoever sends the transaction

levers.label: Busy network
levers.desc: Fees can jump 10–100× in a rush, so a business must budget for peaks.

levers.label: Layer 2
levers.desc: Rollups such as Arbitrum or Base run the same contract for a fraction of the fee.

gas.ladderPrompt: Which operation costs the most? Tap your guess.
gas.ladderExplain: Deploying stores every byte of code on every node forever, and writing data is the next most expensive thing a contract does. Reading is free.
gas.ladderNote: Bars are illustrative, not to scale.

why.heading: Why can't a smart contract just check the weather?
why.subtitle: It can hold a million dollars and pay out in seconds, yet it cannot look up a single fact outside its own chain.
why.pickHint: Tap anything the contract needs to know
items: Rainfall today
ETH price
Match result
Flight delay
Any web API
why.idle: Go on, try it: send the contract out to fetch something.
why.blocked: blocked. Contract code runs inside a sealed virtual machine with no internet, no file system and no API calls. It can read only what is already on its own chain.
why.thoughtTitle: What if every node called the API itself?
why.noConsensus: Three nodes, three answers: no consensus, no block.
why.thoughtBody: Thousands of nodes re-run every contract and must reach the identical result. A live API answers each of them a little differently. The wall is deliberate: it is what keeps every node in agreement.
why.bridge: So how does an insurance contract ever learn that it did not rain?

what.heading: What is an oracle?
what.subtitle: The bridge between a smart contract and the real world. You placed one in the stack exercise: Chainlink.
what.toggleLabel: Same contract, same drought — flip the switch
what.def: A service that fetches data from outside the blockchain and writes it on-chain, so that smart contracts can read it and act on it.
what.nuance: The contract still never reaches out. The oracle pushes the data in as an ordinary transaction, and from then on every node reads the same stored value. The sandbox stays intact.

how.heading: How does the data get on-chain?
how.subtitle: Four steps, and one design rule: never rely on a single reporter.

steps.label: Fetch
steps.desc: Oracle nodes, computers outside the chain, pull the value from several sources: exchanges, weather services, APIs.

steps.label: Report
steps.desc: Each node signs its answer and reports it.

steps.label: Aggregate
steps.desc: The answers are combined into one value, usually the median, so a few outliers cannot move it.

steps.label: Read
steps.desc: The value is stored in an on-chain feed contract. Your contract reads it like any other on-chain data.

how.labPrompt: Tap a node to make it lie. How many liars does it take to fool the contract?

status.honest: Every report is honest. The feed is right.
status.tolerated: {{n}} of 5 nodes lying. The median ignores the outliers, so the feed is still right.
status.captured: A majority is lying, so the median itself is a lie. The contract will act on $9,999.
status.singleOk: It works, for as long as this one machine stays honest, online and unhacked.
status.singleBad: One oracle, one lie. The feed is wrong and nothing on-chain can tell.

how.note: its price feeds work this way. Many independent node operators and many data sources produce one aggregated value on-chain, refreshed when the price moves enough or a timer runs out.

risks.heading: The oracle problem
risks.subtitle: A blockchain can verify signatures and arithmetic. It cannot verify whether a number is true.
risks.pickHint: Pick a failure to see which link breaks

items.title: Single point of failure
items.desc: One node or one company supplies the data. If it goes offline, gets hacked or is bribed, every contract that depends on it fails with it.
items.effect: No data arrives. The contract is stuck, and so is the money inside it.
items.defense: Many independent nodes and many sources.

items.title: Stale or wrong data
items.tagline: A true number, six hours too late.
items.desc: The feed stops updating during an outage or network congestion, or a source publishes a mistake. The contract keeps acting on a number that is no longer true.
items.effect: It lends and liquidates at a price the market left behind.
items.defense: Check the data's timestamp and pause when it is too old.

items.title: Manipulation
items.tagline: An honest messenger carrying a lie.
items.desc: The oracle reports faithfully, but someone has bent the source itself: a thinly traded market, a single sensor. The false number arrives on-chain properly signed.
items.effect: It pays out on a number that someone engineered.
items.defense: Combine deep markets, average over time, reject outliers.

risks.paradox: Smart contracts remove the trusted middleman from the deal, then let one back in through the data feed. A contract is only as trustworthy as its data source.
risks.next: Next: two real cases, a thermometer in Paris and a price tag worth millions.

paris.heading: How hot was it in Paris? That depends on which thermometer you ask.
paris.subtitle: A prediction market paid out on one airport sensor. Then that sensor showed a spike nobody else saw.
paris.outcomeSensor: Daily high: 22°C. The long-shot bet wins.
paris.outcomeNearby: Daily high: about 18°C. The favourite wins.
paris.chartNote: 6 April 2026, temperature levels as reported; the shape of the curve is illustrative.

facts.label: The rule
facts.text: Polymarket ran a daily market on the highest temperature in Paris. Its rules settled it on one Météo-France sensor at Charles de Gaulle airport. That sensor was the oracle.

facts.label: The spike
facts.text: On 6 and 15 April its reading jumped by more than 3°C for a few minutes, then fell back. Nearby stations showed no such spike.

facts.label: The payout
facts.text: Long-shot bets on exactly those readings collected more than $35,000.

facts.label: The aftermath
facts.text: Météo-France filed a police complaint for interference with its equipment. Polymarket moved the Paris market to a sensor at Le Bourget airport.

paris.status: Tampering is suspected, not proven: the investigation was still open when this was reported.
paris.lesson: The market paid exactly as written: whatever that one sensor said. "The temperature in Paris" had to be defined as one device, and whoever can touch the device can move the payout. An oracle is a trust and definition problem, not only a technical one.
paris.sources: Reported by NPR, CNN, Euronews and Decrypt, April 2026.

attack.heading: How do you rob a lender by changing a price tag?
attack.subtitle: The classic DeFi oracle attack: bend the price in a small market, then cash in at a bigger one that trusts it.

steps.label: Setup
steps.what: Market B lends dollars to anyone who posts TOKEN as collateral. To know what TOKEN is worth, its contract reads the live price from Market A, a small trading pool.

steps.label: Flash loan
steps.what: The attacker borrows $2M with no collateral at all. The catch: a flash loan must be repaid inside the same transaction, or the whole transaction is cancelled.

steps.label: Pump
steps.what: The attacker pours the $2M into Market A, buying TOKEN. That much buying in so small a pool drives the price from $1 to $4. The attacker now holds 1M TOKEN.

steps.label: Trust
steps.what: The attacker posts the 1M TOKEN at Market B as collateral. The contract asks its oracle for the price, hears $4 and books the collateral at $4M. It has no way of knowing the price is fake.

steps.label: Drain
steps.what: Against $4M of collateral on paper, Market B lends out $3M in real dollars, its usual 75%.

steps.label: Exit
steps.what: The attacker repays the $2M flash loan and walks away with $1M. The pool price sinks back to about $1, so Market B holds collateral worth about $1M against a $3M loan. One transaction, a few seconds.

safeSteps: The attacker posts the 1M TOKEN at Market B. This oracle averages many markets over time, so one small pool barely moves it: it still says about $1. The collateral is booked at about $1M.
Against $1M of collateral, Market B lends at most $0.75M.
The attacker owes $2M and holds $0.75M. The flash loan cannot be repaid, so the whole transaction is cancelled: no loan, no trade, nothing happened. The attempt costs only gas.
attack.toggleLabel: Try it: which price does Market B trust?
attack.real: bZx (2020), Harvest Finance (2020), Mango Markets (2022, about $110M).
attack.footnote: Numbers here are illustrative; fees ignored.

reshape.heading: How Smart Contracts Reshape Traditional Business
reshape.subtitle: Five structural shifts.
reshape.imgAlt: Two people exchanging documents directly — disintermediation

viz.label: One deal, two routes — flip the switch

cards.title: Disintermediation
cards.desc: Peer-to-peer execution. No banks, brokers, or escrow services needed for the agreement to clear.

cards.title: Process Automation
cards.desc: Autonomous "if X, then Y" rules execute the moment conditions are met — no manual approval step.

cards.title: Trustless & Transparent
cards.desc: Trust shifts from people to code + consensus. All actions are verifiable, auditable, and global. Once deployed, no party can change the rules, including the issuer.

cards.title: Cost Reduction
cards.desc: Eliminates middlemen, manual paperwork, and ongoing legal oversight. Cuts escrow, reconciliation, and compliance costs.

cards.title: New Value Chains
cards.desc: New models: DAOs, tokenised assets, machine-to-machine payments.

reshape.patternBody: traditional businesses centralise trust in an intermediary; smart-contract businesses move it into code and consensus. Build one when many parties must share one record without a referee; otherwise a database is cheaper. The next section shows where this works in practice.

quiz.question: The conditions written into a deployed smart contract are finally met. What actually makes its code run?
options: A timer inside the contract that checks its conditions at set intervals
A transaction that someone sends, calling one of its functions
The contract itself: it executes automatically the moment the conditions are met
A validator who notices that the conditions are met and triggers it
quiz.explanation: A contract never acts on its own: it has no timer and cannot watch the world. It sits idle until a signed transaction calls one of its functions, directly or through another contract. Only then does it run its checks, update state and emit events, all within that one transaction.

quiz2.question: In the escrow walkthrough, a stranger (not the buyer) calls deposit() with 2 ETH. What happens?
options: The contract keeps the 2 ETH but leaves the deal marked Unpaid
The transaction reverts, nothing changes, and the stranger's gas is refunded
The transaction reverts, nothing changes, and the stranger still pays the gas
The transaction stays pending until the real buyer approves it
quiz2.explanation: The contract checks its rules before anything moves. A failed check reverts the whole transaction: balances, status and events stay exactly as they were, so nothing half-happens. The nodes still did the work of running it, so the gas already used is not refunded.

quiz3.question: A crop-insurance contract must pay out when rainfall is below 10 mm. Why can't the contract simply call a weather API itself?
options: Every node re-runs the contract and must get the identical result; a live API could answer each node differently
Calling an API would cost more gas than most contracts can afford
Weather data is too large to fit inside a block
It can, but only through APIs that the validators have approved in advance
quiz3.explanation: Contract code runs in a sealed virtual machine on thousands of nodes, and all of them must reach the same result. A live API could answer each node differently, so outside calls are simply not available. An oracle solves this by writing the data on-chain in a transaction; from then on every node reads the same stored value.

quiz4.question: A lending protocol values collateral using the live price from one small trading pool. An attacker pushes that price up 4× for a few seconds and borrows against the inflated collateral. What was the root weakness?
options: A bug in the lending contract's code miscalculated the loan
Flash loans make it possible to borrow without collateral
The validators failed to spot and reject the fake price
The contract trusted a single price source that was cheap to manipulate
quiz4.explanation: The lending contract ran exactly as written, and validators only check that the rules were followed, not that a price is fair. The weakness was the oracle design: one small pool is cheap to move, even for a few seconds. Flash loans merely make the attack cheaper to fund. Safer feeds combine many markets and average over time.

takeaways.title: Section 02 — Key Takeaways
items: A dApp is a full stack: only the contract layer is decentralised, the rest are ordinary servers
Five words describe any contract: code, state, functions, events and the platform it runs on
Every run is the same loop: a transaction calls a function, the code checks its rules, state changes, an event fires
A failed check reverts everything — nothing half-happens
Every node computes the same result, and that work is paid for in gas by whoever sends the transaction
The business effect: programmable money and automated settlement with no middleman to pay or trust
A contract cannot see the outside world: oracles write real-world data on-chain, and the contract is only as safe as that data

keyPoints.s2-web3: Web3 moves trust from the company running the service to the rules running the network.
keyPoints.s2-dapp: The blockchain is one layer of a dApp; the website, data feeds and storage are ordinary servers that someone controls.
keyPoints.s2-ex-stack: Only the contract is decentralised by default; every other box is a vendor you depend on.
keyPoints.s2-vs: Web2 apps can change the rules overnight; Web3 apps make the rules public and hard to change.
keyPoints.s2-components: Code, state, functions, events, platform: five words that let you follow any contract summary.
keyPoints.s2-workflow: A transaction, not a person, triggers the contract, and the result is final on every node.
keyPoints.s2-run: A contract does nothing until someone calls it; then it checks, updates and announces, the same way for everyone.
keyPoints.s2-solidity: A contract is readable code, not a black box; you can ask a vendor to show it.
keyPoints.s2-execution: Thousands of machines compute the same result, which makes it trustworthy, slow, expensive and public.
keyPoints.s2-capabilities: The new capability is automation that no single party, including the operator, can override.
keyPoints.s2-liquidity: A lending pool turns idle crypto into yield: borrowers pay the interest, and code, not a bank, sits in the middle.
keyPoints.s2-flash: A flash loan is safe for the lender for one reason: the transaction repays it in full, or it never happened.
keyPoints.s2-gas: Every step costs real money, so good design keeps heavy data off-chain and puts only the proof on-chain.
keyPoints.s2-standards: Standards are why one wallet works with thousands of tokens.
keyPoints.s2-oracle-why: A smart contract is blind by design: it sees only what is already on its own chain.
keyPoints.s2-oracle-what: An oracle does not make a contract smarter; it puts outside facts on-chain where the contract can read them.
keyPoints.s2-oracle-how: Many reporters and a median replace "trust this one company" with "trust that most of them are honest".
keyPoints.s2-oracle-risks: The chain executes faithfully on whatever the oracle says: wrong data in, wrong payout out.
keyPoints.s2-oracle-paris: Before trusting an automated payout, ask which exact source decides, and who can touch it.
keyPoints.s2-oracle-attack: A smart contract is only as safe as the oracle feeding it.
keyPoints.s2-reshape: Smart-contract businesses stop earning as the trusted middleman; the revenue model moves.
